# The 'sustainability-data' Well-Known URI (IETF Internet-Draft)

> A uniform, out-of-band convention for web servers and digital services to publish their environmental impact, energy consumption, and carbon footprint metrics.

## Project Links
* **GitHub Repository:** https://github.com/andreibesleaga/rfc-sustainability-wellknown
* **IETF Datatracker:** https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-besleaga-sustainability-wellknown/
* **Author:** Andrei Nicolae Besleaga (https://github.com/andreibesleaga)
* **IETF Stream:** Independent Submission (individual; not a working-group product)
* **Current Draft Status:** `-11`, **posted 2026-10-27** to the Datatracker (the latest posted revision, under ISE review). It shortens four passages at the Independent Submissions Editor's comments on `-10` and keeps the `-10` wire format, so a `-10` document is a valid `-11` document. `-10` (posted 2026-10-24) changed the wire format at the Independent Submissions Editor's suggestions on `-09` (posted 2026-10-16): every date is an RFC 3339 `date-time` (`period` is an object `{start, end}`, half-open; the `start` and `end` query parameters are UTC date-times), and `measurement-method` (4 tokens), `functional-unit` (12), `target-type` (9), the `upstream` `role` (6) and `carbon-unit` (`gCO2e`, `kgCO2e`, `tCO2e`) are closed sets; the recommended signature algorithm is `Ed25519`. A `-09` document is not a valid `-10` document. `-09` replaced `reporting-period` and the `period` query parameter, restructured the document and removed the aggregation and `400`/`404` query rules. `-08` (posted 2026-10-09) changed no wire format. The paragraph that follows describes `-07` (posted 2026-09-17). It withdraws the companion `/.well-known/sustainability-data.jws` resource and its detached signature entirely — no legacy support, no redirect, no fallback — replacing it with an OPTIONAL `signed` member embedded in each declaration object; removes the `version` member, leaving exactly seven mandatory members; closes the top-level member set and moves private extensions into an OPTIONAL `extensions` object keyed by absolute URI (RFC 3986) instead of reverse-domain top-level names; adds an OPTIONAL `upstream` member linking to the declarations a subject's figures derive from; replaces the old free/unauthenticated-methodology conformance floor with a simpler "at least one numeric metric, `disclosure-uri`, or `verifiable-attestation-uri`" rule; gives Extended Query Parameters an ABNF grammar and a numbered processing procedure with defined `400`/`404` cases; drops the server-side 366-object cap in favor of a consumer-side byte/object bound; and drops the `X-Content-Type-Options` recommendation from the specification text.
* **`-06`** (posted 2026-09-10): an earlier posted revision. It responds to the ISE's second round (security designed in from the start) and to the first commissioned review: it requests registration of the `application/sustainability-data+json` media type in the standards tree and requires it, makes HTTPS a MUST, adds an OPTIONAL detached-JWS signature mechanism at a companion well-known resource, restructures the Security Considerations around a threat-model table, adds a "Roles and Processing Model" section and a "Partial Knowledge and Incremental Adoption" section, and fixes the `version` label as a single defined value — all with no wire-format change from `-05`. (`-07`, above, supersedes the detached-JWS, `version`, and `nosniff` points of this paragraph; this remains an accurate record of what `-06` shipped.)
* **`-05`** (posted 2026-07-28): responded to the ISE's initial review of `-04` — removing the carbon.txt-path reference from `disclosure-uri` (now format- and location-agnostic), adding an Internationalization Considerations section, and recognizing the calendar year as the common Basic-service reporting cycle — with no wire-format change.
* **`-04`** (also posted): renamed the requested well-known URI suffix from `sustainability` to `sustainability-data` (per ISE feedback on RFC 8615's precision expectations, resolving the IANA well-known-URI naming feedback), added the optional `target-type` member, placed the `version` value space under change control, and defined the reverse-domain extension-member naming rule. `-03` (posted 2026-07-23) is an earlier posted revision.

## Context and Purpose
The digital economy consumes a significant percentage of global electricity. Regulatory frameworks (like the EU CSRD) and industry standards (like GSF SCI, W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines) increasingly require organizations to disclose their digital environmental impact. 

An earlier per-request HTTP-header approach to carbon transparency was explored first — filed as `draft-besleaga-green-sustainability-header-00` (now expired) — and set aside in favor of this well-known URI's out-of-band design, which avoids the per-request "rebound effect" (metadata increasing the footprint it reports). This project proposes an alternative: leveraging RFC 8615 to define a discoverable `/.well-known/sustainability-data` URI for asynchronous, out-of-band reporting. This allows workflows where environmental impact is a primary constraint alongside cost and performance.

**Applicability is broader than conventional websites.** RFC 8615 well-known URIs are scoped to an HTTP(S) *origin* (scheme+host+port), not to "a website" — any HTTP-speaking device or service can serve one. That includes IoT/embedded devices (constrained devices already use the analogous convention, CoAP's `/.well-known/core`, registered by RFC 6690) and Web3/blockchain infrastructure (an RPC gateway or validator dashboard is an ordinary HTTP origin). The data model is entity-level, not hosting-level: `provider` names the operating entity, and the reference implementation's enterprise adapters (Salesforce NZC, Microsoft Sustainability Manager, Watershed) are written to populate documents from organization-level reporting platforms rather than server telemetry; they run in the gateway against recorded responses, none has been exercised against a live tenant, and the Microsoft adapter targets a preview API retired 2025-05-30 — so the same endpoint can carry a regulator-mandated organizational disclosure (e.g. EU CSRD, or the EU MiCA consensus-mechanism energy/carbon disclosure already required of crypto-asset issuers), not only a website's own hosting footprint.

## Repository Structure & Resources
In addition to tracking the evolution of the draft through standard IETF versions (the former `draft-besleaga-green-sustainability-wellknown-00`…`-05` series, continued as `draft-besleaga-sustainability-wellknown-00`…`-10`, of which `-10` (posted 2026-10-24) is the latest posted revision), the GitHub repository acts as an extended resource hub for implementers. It includes:
* **Draft Sources (`internet-drafts/`):** The core `.md` (Markdown) files which act as the source documents compiled into the final IETF `.xml`/`.txt` formats using the kramdown-rfc + xml2rfc toolchains, plus a `CHANGELOG.md` and a supplementary W3C Verifiable Credential structure.
* **Schemas & Validators (`schemas-validators/`):** Formal machine-readable definitions of the JSON data model — JSON Type Definition (JTD, RFC 8927) and Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL, RFC 8610) — with Python (JTD) and Ruby (CDDL, gem 0.12.14) validators and a `validate-all.sh` runner.
* **Examples (`example-responses/`):** 42 sample JSON responses (the example corpus with valid, tolerated and invalid cases is in `schemas-validators/examples/`, listed in a manifest) demonstrating Basic, Extended, Target-Specific, and annual-reporting scenarios — including origin/organization/service/product/device/tenant/data-source `target-type` examples, the `upstream` pair (a downstream organization and the tenant-scoped declaration it names), and a minimum-conformance example, and a comprehensive data-centre-operator report carrying every optional member that fits an organization plus six `https`-keyed extensions (facility ISO/IEC 30134 KPIs, water, waste, hardware circularity, direct emissions, renewable procurement). All pass both validators.
* **Reference Implementation (`publisher/`):** A reference TypeScript publisher that serves a conformant `/.well-known/sustainability-data` from pluggable source adapters (static/computed, Kepler/Prometheus, Climatiq, Green Web Foundation CO2.js [bytes→carbon], the Green Web Foundation carbon.txt hosted API, Salesforce Net Zero Cloud, Microsoft Sustainability Manager, Watershed). It normalizes units, validates every payload against the JTD schema (plus prose checks) before serving; the CDDL is checked by `validate-all.sh` and CI, and ships as Express/Fastify middleware and a standalone server. It can also serve a bidirectional `carbon.txt` (emit/parse/discover helper) that points back to the metrics document. Includes example security middleware (`example-scripts/`) and web-server configs (`server-configurations/`). Published on npm as **`sustainability-wellknown-publisher`** (registry 0.1.0 implements the historical -02/"1.1" model; 0.4.0 through 0.6.7 implement the "2.0" model; **0.8.2 is the current release and implements `-10`** (0.8.0 was the first); 0.7.0 to 0.7.3 implemented `-07`'s payload changes — the embedded `signed` member replacing the detached JWS, the closed member set, `extensions`, and `upstream` — with fixes and the CSV and Slurm adapters; `0.6.0` had added the `-06` media type and HTTPS, and `0.6.5` had added the (now withdrawn) detached-JWS signature, the vc+jwt attestation, and the consumer's --verify).
* **Reference Client (`consumer/`):** A TypeScript reference *client* for `/.well-known/sustainability-data`, complementing the publisher's reference *producer*. It fetches a document from any origin, defensively validates it (JTD schema plus this package's prose checks: start before end, at-least-one-metric, the sci-score dependency, the day floor and the URI forms), transforms it (CSV, NDJSON, a flattened one-row-per-metric shape, a total over non-overlapping periods), and doubles as a standalone conformance checker (its `sustainability-fetch --strict` CLI). It ships a zero-dependency one-call `fetchSustainability` function and a richer ETag-caching `SustainabilityClient` class, and is interop-tested in-process against a real `Publisher` — demonstrating the full produce→fetch→validate→transform lifecycle across two independent implementations. Published on npm as **`sustainability-wellknown-consumer`** (same versioning note as the publisher).
* **Supporting Docs:** `ADOPTION.md` (the case for RFC/IANA adoption) and `sfc-compliance/` — the checker (`sfc-check.mjs`), JSON Schemas, test vectors and examples for SFC profile 2.0. The profile text is the single spec at https://github.com/andreibesleaga/awesome-blockchain-greentech/blob/main/Innovative%20Projects/SFC_COMPLIANCE.md; `sfc-compliance/PROFILE.md` only points to it.

## Key Technical Specifications

### The Endpoint
* **Path:** `/.well-known/sustainability-data`
* **Method:** HTTP GET and HEAD, the only methods the draft uses; method handling and status codes are as RFC 9110 defines them (the draft cites it rather than restating `405`/`Allow`)
* **Protocol:** HTTPS (MUST)
* **Response:** `200 OK` with `application/sustainability-data+json` payload; a consumer MAY also process a `200 OK` whose `Content-Type` is `application/json`, and a response carrying any other media type is not a declaration. Access control, caching and every other aspect of the HTTP exchange are as RFC 9110 and RFC 9111 define them and are the publisher's to configure. Publishers follow I-JSON (RFC 7493). An origin that publishes no declaration has no representation at the URI.

### Query Parameters
A server MAY support the query parameters `target`, `start`, `end` and `granularity` (RFC 3986 query component, `name=value`). A server that does not support a parameter ignores it and answers the rest of the request, so a static file satisfies every request; a plain static file is the common case. `start`, `end` and `granularity` have an ABNF grammar (RFC 5234, RFC 7405):
* `start`, `end`: a UTC RFC 3339 `date-time` ending in `Z`, such as `2025-01-01T00:00:00Z`. A server that honors them and receives a value that does not match the grammar ignores the parameter and never reads it as another value (there is no `400`).
* `granularity`: `yearly`, `monthly` or `daily`. An object satisfies it when its period is a whole calendar year, month or day respectively.
* `target`: a `target` member value (a path prefix begins with "/"). An object satisfies it when its `target` equals the value.
* A server that supports the parameters returns the objects it holds that satisfy every parameter it honors, as a JSON array in ascending order of `period.start` (compared as instants); when none does, the array is empty (`200`, not `404`). An object satisfies `start` and `end` when its period overlaps the range: its `period.start` is before `end` and its `period.end` after `start`. A server returns what it holds, as it holds it, and computes no aggregate. Because a server may ignore any parameter, a consumer MUST compare the `period` and `target` of every object it receives with what it requested and MUST NOT record a response as covering a period or target it does not name.

**Key distinction:** the *origin* is where the document is published; the `target` member is what the metrics are about — they coincide for origin-wide reports (the origin's host), but `target` may equally name an organization, a path, a cloud tenant, a device, or a data source.

### Data Model
Since `-07`, and still in `-10`, the response schema defines 7 mandatory + 19 optional members (26 total); the `version` member of `-04`–`-06` (fixed at `"2.0"`) is removed and the media type alone identifies the format:
* **Mandatory Fields (7):**
  * `updated`: RFC 3339 `date-time` of last update (`T` and `Z` in upper case).
  * `capabilities`: "basic" when the server supports no query parameter, "extended" when it supports at least one (a "basic" document MAY carry any optional members).
  * `provider`: Information about the publisher.
  * `measurement-method`: one of four tokens, from the most to the least direct: `hardware-metered`, `hardware-estimated`, `cloud-billing`, `third-party-modeled`.
  * `methodology-uri`: a URI reference to a document for people that describes the method.
  * `period`: an object `{"start", "end"}`, each an RFC 3339 `date-time`, from `start` (included) to `end` (excluded); `start` MUST be before `end`. Calendar 2025 is `{"start": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`. Whole calendar years and months are RECOMMENDED; a period SHOULD be a calendar day or longer.
  * `target`: Opaque identifier of what the object is about — a protocol element compared as a string and never translated — origin host (RECOMMENDED for origin-wide reports), path prefix, organizational entity, cloud tenant, or software data source.
* **Optional Fields (19):** `target-type` (classifies the target, one of nine: `organization`, `facility`, `origin`, `path`, `service`, `product`, `device`, `tenant`, `data-source`), `energy-consumption` (non-negative) & `energy-unit` (Wh, kWh, MWh, GWh; default `kWh` when absent), `carbon-footprint` (gross, non-negative) & `carbon-unit` (gCO2e, kgCO2e, tCO2e; default `gCO2e` when absent, also parameterizing scopes), `carbon-accounting` (location/market-based), `scope-1`, `scope-2`, `scope-3` emissions (MAY be negative — removals/net accounting), `sci-score` (non-negative; requires `functional-unit`), `functional-unit` (one of twelve: `per-request`, `per-transaction`, `per-page-view`, `per-session`, `per-user`, `per-job`, `per-token`, `per-inference`, `per-gigabyte`, `per-gigabyte-hour`, `per-vcpu-hour`, `per-device`), `carbon-intensity-gCO2e-per-kWh`, `estimated-annual-emissions-kgCO2e`, `renewable-energy` percentage (0–100 inclusive), `verifiable-attestation-uri` (at most one per declaration; a subject with more than one attestation links an index of them from `disclosure-uri`), `disclosure-uri` (a format- and location-agnostic URI reference to a machine-readable sustainability disclosure index; the Green Web Foundation's carbon.txt convention is one such form among others, cited as complementary work), `upstream` (array of `{ declaration: <URI reference to another declaration>, role?: hosting/colocation/cloud/cdn/network/electricity }` — declarations a subject's figures derive from; a consumer MAY walk the chain to depth 3, no revisits, comparing same-period figures as evidence, never proof), `extensions` (object keyed by URI, RFC 3986 — a URI under the definer's control, or a UUID URN, RFC 9562, for a definer without a domain; a key is an identifier compared as a string, never dereferenced, and there is no registry; a consumer that does not implement a key's definition ignores its value and never dereferences or executes anything within it), and `signed` (the embedded JWS — see Signing below).
* **Minimum reporting rule:** a declaration object MUST carry at least one numeric metric member, or `disclosure-uri`, or `verifiable-attestation-uri`; an object with none of the three is not conformant. (The `-06` condition requiring the `methodology-uri` resource itself to be free and unauthenticated when no metric was present is removed in `-07`.)
* **Closed top-level member set:** a publisher MUST NOT add other top-level members; a consumer ignores one it does not recognize. Private extension data goes in `extensions` (above), not as an additional top-level member.
* **Omitted metrics & legacy compatibility:** omission is the only "not reported" mechanism — no in-band sentinel exists. Historical `1.x` documents used a negative sentinel and an optional `target-path` member. The packages (not the specification) additionally tolerate historical documents: they apply field-driven compatibility/tolerance rules (a negative value in a non-negative member = not reported; a wrong-JSON-type value, including `null`, = not reported/absent; an `sci-score` without `functional-unit` = absent; a missing `target` = origin-wide report; a legacy document carrying `target-path` = metrics attributed to that declared subject, not the origin). From 0.8.0 the consumer's compatibility reading also converts the `-08` and `-09` forms (`reporting-period`, date-only `period` bounds, earlier token values), reporting each change as converted or disregarded; strict mode reads a document exactly as served.
* **Readiness (by design):** web-ready (plain HTTPS GET, standard caching/conditional requests), API/M2M-ready (stable JSON + formal CDDL/JTD schemas + deterministic semantics), human-readable (self-describing member names + mandatory methodology link), and AI/agent-ready (fixed discoverable location, schema-validatable, no content negotiation needed).

### Signing (the `signed` member, since `-07`)
Each declaration object MAY carry an OPTIONAL `signed` member: a JWS Compact Serialization whose payload is that same object minus `signed`, with protected header `alg` (`Ed25519`, RFC 9864, or `ES256` are RECOMMENDED; `none` and MACs MUST NOT be used; the former identifier `EdDSA` is still verified by the reference consumer, with a note), `cty: "sustainability-data+json"`, and the key as `jwk`/`x5c`/`kid`. A consumer verifies it only when present — absence means unsigned, never an error. Precedence depends on how far the key is trusted: where it was obtained out of band, pinned from an earlier retrieval, or chained through `x5c` to a trusted anchor, the verified payload's values are the ones used; in every other case the key is trusted no further than the declaration carrying it and the members the origin served remain the ones used (pinning gives continuity of authorship, not identity). Either way a mismatch is reported as "modified after signing", not a verification failure. `-07` withdraws the `-06`-era companion resource `/.well-known/sustainability-data.jws` and its detached signature entirely: there is no legacy support, no redirect, no fallback.

## Important Considerations
* **Caching & DoS:** Access control and caching are the publisher's to configure under RFC 9110 and RFC 9111. The draft bounds the *consumer*: it SHOULD bound the time, size and redirects of every fetch and refuse loopback, private and link-local addresses at every connection, MUST limit the bytes and objects it accepts, and in an upstream walk MUST bound depth, revisits and the total number of retrievals. The reference publisher can also cap the number of objects it holds (366 is illustrated) as a deployment safeguard and refuses to start above it; it never truncates an answer.
* **Privacy & Traffic Analysis:** A period SHOULD be a calendar day or longer (each bound the first instant of a calendar day in its own offset) to prevent correlating energy spikes with real-time user actions.
* **Hardware Fingerprinting:** An optional ~1% multiplicative (sign-preserving) "fuzzing" of metrics helps obscure specific backend hardware architectures with limited impact on aggregate accuracy; if applied, it is applied once at generation time, deterministically per period, and consistently across related fields — non-negative members stay non-negative and negative scope values keep their sign.
* **Greenwashing Mitigation:** The specification does not mandate verification but provides schema surfaces (like `verifiable-attestation-uri`) to link to cryptographically signed W3C Verifiable Credentials or third-party attestations.
* **Text and comparison (the Internationalization Considerations section was removed in `-10`; each rule now sits with the member it governs):** the body is UTF-8 JSON; strings are compared as the same sequence of Unicode characters once JSON escapes are decoded, with no case folding; `target` is never translated and an internationalized host is written in A-label form; `provider` is text in any script, and a publisher states its language with `Content-Language`.

## Extensibility & Versioning
* **The `version` member is removed as of `-07`.** `-04` through `-06` carried it as an informational label, fixed by `-06` at the single value `"2.0"`; the media type alone now identifies the format, and there is no version member at all to be informational about.
* **The top-level member set is closed.** A publisher MUST NOT add other top-level members; a consumer ignores one it does not recognize, with a warning. Forward compatibility for the *defined* member set still rests on the must-ignore rule for members a future revision of the specification adds.
* **Private extensions live in the OPTIONAL `extensions` object, keyed by a URI** (RFC 3986), replacing the `-04`–`-06` reverse-domain-name convention (`com.example.pue`) and the "undotted names reserved for the specification" rule. Two forms are used in practice: an `https` URI under the definer's control when the name was minted, and `urn:uuid:` followed by a UUID (RFC 9562) for a definer that has no domain or wants a name independent of one. The name identifies the party that defines its value's members; the definer chooses it once and publishes the definition wherever it chooses. Keys are compared as strings after JSON escapes are decoded, and are never dereferenced — so a later change of domain ownership does not change what an existing document means — and no registry is defined. The model is RFC 7519's Collision-Resistant Name and RFC 8288's extension relation types. A publisher's methodology document SHOULD list the extension names it uses with their definitions. A consumer that does not implement a name's definition MUST ignore that value and MUST NOT dereference or execute anything within it. (`-10` drops the lowercase-scheme and UUID-case rules, and the Nil/Max exclusion: a name is a URI compared as a string.)
* New top-level members can still only be introduced by a future revision of this specification, under the must-ignore rule; private, un-standardized data always goes inside `extensions`, never as a new top-level name.
